## About — Dario Espinosa · Lead Experience Designer
URL: https://datadaeon.github.io/about.html
Summary: Dario Espinosa — Lead Experience Designer with 18+ years building digital products. Specializing in design systems, accessibility, AI-assisted design, and enterprise UX.

Lead Experience Designer · Chiapas MX

## Design is
Everything.

18+ years turning complex systems into clear, human experiences, from enterprise telecom to AI-powered tools and immersive spatial design.

Available for new opportunities

Get in touch

About

I'm Dario Espinosa, a Lead Experience Designer who turns complex, outdated systems into clear, human solutions that drive real business impact.

Great design combines strategy, creativity, and execution. Every decision research-driven, built shoulder-to-shoulder with stakeholders and engineering.

Accessibility and innovation aren't add-ons. They've earned international recognition. My principle never changes: understand the system before you redesign it.

18+

Years of experience

40+

Enterprise components

9

Industry verticals

ES

Español · Native

EN

English · B2

Multidisciplinary Experience Designer with 18+ years shipping across field operations, industrial software, enterprise platforms, and healthcare products — from startups to Fortune 500 companies.

I prototype in code using Claude and coding agents , which means stakeholders see a working interface, not a static mockup, from the first review. Research-grounded, systems-minded — I like taking a complex legacy system apart and turning it into something people can actually use, in ways that show up in the numbers.

Based in Chiapas, MX . Recognized with the 2020 AT&T International Accessibility in Action Award for inclusive design at national scale. Currently at SoftServe spanning healthcare, construction SaaS, analytics, and emerging tech (XR / Metaverse).

Design & prototyping: Figma, Affinity, Sketch, Adobe CC, AEM, Penpot. AI agents & dev: Claude, Cursor, local LLMs. Research: Miro, Maze, UserTesting, HotJar.

Comprehensive information frameworks that enhance usability. Design systems that ensure consistency and efficiency across large digital products.

I bring strategic vision to digital experiences: brand consistency, visual storytelling, and design leadership that connects product with identity.

#### AI-Native Prototyping

I prototype in code with Claude and coding agents, so stakeholders review a working interface from the first session and decisions get tested, not just presented.

## Ascend Restyle — A Skill That Redesigns Portfolio Decks · Dario Espinosa
URL: https://datadaeon.github.io/ascend-restyle.html
Summary: Ascend Restyle — a Claude Agent Skill built for an internal UX Center of Excellence that restyles a designer's existing portfolio or bio deck into the firm's internal design system, producing an annotatable HTML preview before export to PPTX or PDF.

internal tool · claude skill · ux coe

## Ascend Restyle — A Skill That
Redesigns Portfolio Decks On Its Own

A Claude Agent Skill built for an internal UX Center of Excellence: point it at a designer's existing portfolio or bio deck (PDF, PowerPoint, or Keynote export) and it restyles the whole thing into the firm's internal design system , then hands back an annotatable HTML preview so the designer can polish content before exporting a final PPTX or PDF.

context
Internal Tool · UX CoE

role
Creator · Skill Author

format
Claude Agent Skill

tested on
My own portfolio

49 source pages restyled

4 layout archetypes

7 pipeline steps

0 rounded corners

01 — Overview

Self-Initiated · UX CoE

### The Problem: Every Designer's Deck Looks Different

Designers at the firm carry portfolio decks built up over years: different templates, different tools, different eras of personal style. Every time the UX CoE needed one presented internally or to a client, someone spent hours by hand rebuilding slides into the current brand system, one shape and font at a time.

Ascend Restyle exists to remove that hours-long manual step. It's not a proposal generator, and it doesn't score candidates against a brief. That's what the separate match / export-proposal skills do. This one is a one-to-one restyle: take a designer's own existing material, keep the content, replace the design.

02 — How It Works

### A Seven-Step Restyle Pipeline

The skill is deliberately conservative about content. It never invents or rewrites what a slide says, only how it looks. Structure gets confirmed with the designer before any restyling begins.

STEP 1

Intake
Accepts the source file (PDF, PPTX, or a Keynote export).

STEP 2

Map the structure
Parses every slide/page and confirms the section map with the designer. It never assumes intent.

STEP 3

Restyle in the internal design system
Applies the real design tokens and hard design rules (chamfers, motion, type) to every element.

STEP 3.5

Layout-grid rules
Routes each slide into one of four layout archetypes based on its content density and image count.

STEP 4

Generate the HTML preview
Builds a single browsable preview of the full restyled deck.

STEP 5

Annotation / edit loop
The designer marks up the preview directly with an Agentation toolbar before anything is finalized.

STEP 6–7

Export & completion
Delivered as PPTX and/or PDF (via the pptx skill), or a quick in-browser print-to-PDF for a fast pass.

03 — Target Design System

### Restyling Into the Internal Design System

This is the firm's design language for internal designer-facing material, distinct from client-facing brand work. The skill enforces its real tokens and a short list of hard rules rather than approximating a "similar-looking" theme.

Color tokens

Primary Blue
--ds-primary-100

Accent Orange
--ds-accent-100

Ink
--ds-neutral-600

Type system

Azurio — display headlines

Replica — sans / UI text

Roboto Mono — code & labels

Chamfer-clip corners, never border-radius

Circular status dots are the one exception

No drop shadows or glassmorphism

Motion: 120–220ms cubic-bezier(0.2,0.8,0.2,1)

Why chamfers, not rounded corners

The internal design system deliberately avoids the soft, rounded-corner look most decks default to. Chamfer-clipped polygons give it a sharper, more technical identity that reads as "internal engineering tool" rather than "marketing template," which matches how the UX CoE wants this material to feel.

04 — Real Usage

### Run Against My Own Portfolio

The first real test of the skill was my own 49-page Keynote-exported portfolio PDF: Cover, About, Expertise, Experience, Competence Focus, a Portfolio index, seven full case studies, and a Closing section, all restyled in one pass.

Content correction, not just style

Two real content decisions came up mid-restyle: industry tags across my case studies weren't consistently named, so the skill flagged the inconsistency and we standardized the taxonomy together rather than silently restyling around a mislabeled slide.

A later pass rebuilt the layout engine itself around four grid archetypes driven by content density and image count, so dense case-study slides and sparse cover slides don't get forced into the same template. As of this writing, the preview is generated and the annotation pass is still in progress. That's the honest state of a tool built to be used, not just demoed.

05 — Stack & Tags

### Built On

Claude Agent Skills

.skill packaging

HTML/CSS preview engine

Agentation annotation toolbar

pptx export skill

Internal design-system tokens

ai-tools
design-systems
automation
internal-enablement
ux-coe
founder

#### Style shouldn't be the bottleneck

Content is the hard part. Restyling forty-nine slides shouldn't take longer than writing them did.

## Digital Transformation: AEM & eCommerce Evolution · Dario Espinosa
URL: https://datadaeon.github.io/att.html
Summary: Boosted online sales by 500% and reached 96% accessibility compliance — leading AT&T México's digital transformation through AEM, 40+ custom components, and a complete eCommerce redesign.

Case Study 03

telecommunications

## AEM & eCommerce Evolution

Boosted online sales by 500% and reached 96% accessibility compliance, by leading AT&T México's digital transformation through AEM and a complete eCommerce redesign.

period
5 years

context
AT&T México

role
UX Lead → Manager

tags
AEM eCommerce Accessibility

storefronts and channels, one pipeline

+500%
online sales

96%
accessibility compliance

2020
AT&T a11y award

5yr
engagement history

How Might We

// hmw
unify the digital presence of a multi-brand telecom giant, built from Nextel, Iusacell, and Unefon acquisitions, into a single, accessible, high-converting experience?

The Problem

Every acquisition brought a different tech stack: PHP, AJAX, Flash, CQ5, Drupal. There was no unified design language, no accessibility roadmap, and no shared component library. Users encountered a different AT&T depending on which URL they landed on.

Accessibility was not on anyone's roadmap until regulatory pressure made it unavoidable. The gap between brand promise and digital reality was enormous, and it kept growing with every acquisition.

Visual Context

Illustrative recreation — telecom self-service storefront, generic branding and fictional data

The production storefront and internal UI-toolkit documents are client-confidential. The interactive recreation further down shows the resulting interface without any client-identifying detail.

The Solution

Led the migration from CQ5 to Adobe Experience Manager (AEM) , including a full year of custom component development. It was a long bet, but it paid off in long-term governance and content velocity.

Designed the 2021 AEM design system , then led the migration from Magento 1 to Adobe Commerce . Introduced voice contracts for users with disabilities, one of the first telecom accessibility programs of its kind in México. The 2020 AT&T Accessibility Award followed.

Technical Scope

### 40 Components, One System

The entire system was built for Adobe Experience Manager (AEM) , based on CQ5 (Java) with a database structured around IDs. I had to study directly with Adobe to grasp the development concepts needed to design and deploy the system.

- Created approximately 40 different components for AEM production

- CID (Computer Interaction Design) thinking: technical constraints informed before design decisions

- Atomic Design approach: components built from smaller components, storing information at nodes

- Templates first, then components: mapping what to embed (sliders, rich text, galleries) before building

- Extensive documentation: PPTs and PDFs describing templates, components, character limits, and resize properties

- 2019: a failed deployment. Adobe Brazil and Guatemala teams assisted directly, and we managed a one-year rollback

- 2020–2021: the design system became the foundation for all components across the platform

Role & Responsibilities

### One Designer Across Every Function

Led the design team within Corporate Marketing Operations, operating across multiple concurrent roles throughout the engagement: UX Specialist · UI Designer · Project Manager · Web Design Lead · Content Facilitator.

- Translated AT&T's brand promise, strategy, and design language into world-class digital designs

- Monitored and planned projects with Adobe Brazil teams and agencies

- Managed AEM DAM assets, Information Architecture, and content creation pipeline

- Delivered analytics insights via Adobe Analytics, Google Analytics, and Google Tag Manager

- Managed eCommerce in a separate Magento 2 domain

- Oversaw multiple subdomains and partner initiatives (Netflix, Spotify, Warner, Google)

- Collaborated with Facebook, YouTube, Google, and Twitter on digital strategies

- Maintained AT&T Mexico's national leadership in accessibility, recognized by IFETEL Mexico

- Implemented Agile processes for the web team; trained agencies on UX and accessibility principles

Design System Evolution

### Three Challenges That Shaped the System

Building the first design system for AT&T Mexico required overcoming three foundational challenges that no playbook covered:

- Challenge 1: Finding anyone who had the Digital Guidelines. That meant navigating from Branding to Compliance, speaking with managers and directors across departments

- Challenge 2: Establishing communication with US development and design teams. All files were in Photoshop format, so I had to recreate everything in Sketch, then later migrate to Adobe XD

- Challenge 3: Creating and demonstrating the system as the only designer, frontend developer, and coordinator on the team

Evolution timeline: Initial Sketch system (2016) → Found Adobe XD files from US agency (late 2018) → Full migration to Adobe XD → Left/Right/Viewports approach (desktop top + mobile right) → Modularity allowed live site changes without downtime (2019–2020).

eCommerce Process · D3

### Seguimiento y Atención e-Commerce — 2017

Interactive recreation of the AT&T México internal eCommerce process flow, originally documented in 2017 as the Magento integration went live. Chat agents followed this decision tree to handle order tracking, delivery follow-up, and cancellations. Hover any node.

Key Decision

// design-decision

The implementation required a full year of custom component development. It was a bet on infrastructure over features. Stakeholders wanted faster visible output. Making the case for foundational investment, and holding the line on it, was the critical design leadership moment.

// reflection

Five years across three role changes is unusual for a single engagement. Systems that outlast individual roles require documentation-first thinking from day one. The components I built in year one were still in production when I handed off the system in year five. That's only possible when the rationale is written down, not just lived.

build a scalable, accessible, and consistent design system from zero, in a regulated healthcare environment, without disrupting ongoing product development?

## Modernizing Benefits Software: A Multinational, AI-Assisted Design System · Dario Espinosa
URL: https://datadaeon.github.io/benefits-platform.html
Summary: Leading UX for a from-scratch rebuild of a legacy employee-benefits platform — the code-first, HTML-to-Figma workflow, the multinational team, and the design tokens and KPI framework behind it. WCAG 2.2 AA.

Case Study 08 · Ongoing

enterprise-saas

## Rebuilding Benefits Software

Leading UX for a from-scratch rebuild of a legacy employee-benefits platform used by employers of every size and members of every generation, and building the AI-assisted workflow that let a small, distributed team design, validate and hand off two full portals in a matter of weeks, not quarters.

period
2026 · Ongoing

context
Regulated · Enterprise

role
Lead UX Designer

tags
Design Systems AI Workflow

v1.3→v1.8
iterations shipped

2
portals designed

WCAG 2.2 AA
accessibility bar

3
countries, one team

How Might We

// hmw
replace a decades-old benefits administration system, used by employers of every size and members of every generation, without slowing down a live pilot that stakeholders were already watching closely?

The Problem

The existing platform had grown for years without a dedicated design function. The rules for enrollment, eligibility and rating lived scattered across documents and in the heads of a few long-tenured staff, not in the interface itself.

Roughly a third of the people who would use the new member experience are over 50, and the typical employer admin manages benefits as one responsibility among many, not as a specialist. None of that showed up anywhere in the old product, and it had to show up in the new one.

Reality Check

### A Moving Target, Not a Clean Brief

None of this arrived as one settled brief. Requirements came in through several channels at once: written specs, recorded calls, live workshops. They didn't always agree with each other, either. A rule confirmed in one conversation would get quietly complicated by a document from a different team two weeks later, and it was on us to notice before it reached a screen.

The people pulling on the work wanted different things, too. One senior stakeholder believed AI could handle the design work end to end and treated a design system as overhead. Rather than argue the point, we built the evidence instead: several AI-generated screens for the exact same decision, sitting side by side, all inconsistent with each other. That single comparison did more than any argument would have. It reframed the design system as what makes AI-assisted work land in one consistent place, not a constraint on it.

Other decisions genuinely shifted mid-stream, for good reasons. The accessibility bar got raised on day one once the real user base was understood, an assumed medical-coverage scope narrowed to a firmer dental-and-vision pilot once the actual boundary was confirmed, and more than one piece of member-facing wording got proposed, used, and reversed in the same week once it collided with how that term is actually used in US healthcare. None of that was a planning failure. It's the normal shape of discovery when several people are feeding it at once.

What made it manageable wasn't trying to freeze requirements early. It was accepting that they'd keep moving, and building a habit around that: decide, write it down in one place everyone could check, and move on, instead of relitigating the same question across five different threads.

The Team

### Small, Distributed, Mixed Human and AI

The design team was deliberately small and spread across three countries: a lead UX designer and a second product designer. They worked alongside two AI coding assistants that owned the actual front-end code, plus a separate AI research assistant dedicated to writing, terminology and quality checks.

On the client side, product and business leadership reviewed and signed off on every phase. Rather than one large team in one room, this was a small, mixed group with clearly split responsibilities, which is what let it move fast without losing consistency as more hands touched the same files.

Keeping that many contributors from stepping on each other took an explicit working agreement, not just good intentions. Anything going in front of the client got a tone-and-clarity pass first. Any new word we introduced for what a member would actually read got checked against the official US healthcare glossary before we used it. And any decision that touched a real benefits rule, like waiting periods or eligibility windows, got sanity-checked against how those things actually work in the industry before it ever reached engineering.

Design Workflow

### Code First, Then Figma

Instead of the usual Figma-first process, the team designed in code first. Real, working screens got built in the browser using the same design tokens as the live product, tested with real interaction, and only then captured into Figma automatically, screen by screen.

That order matters: Figma never drifted into an idealized version of the product that didn't match what actually shipped. It stayed a living library of exactly what was built, not a mockup that quietly falls out of date. Designers still worked natively in Figma to compose new screens, but always by reusing real components bound to the same variables running in the product, never by redrawing shapes from scratch.

That flow ran in both directions, deliberately gated. Real screens got captured into Figma automatically so the library always mirrored what actually shipped. Separately, once a component in the Figma library was reviewed and explicitly marked ready, an automated pipeline could generate real front-end code straight from it, wired to the same color, spacing and type variables used in the live product. Nothing got built from a screen that hadn't been signed off as ready. That single checkpoint was what let automation move fast without ever building on work still in flux.

AI-Assisted Workflow

Mixed human + AI team

### Process and Tools, Stage by Stage

Two coding agents owned the front-end code, a dedicated AI research assistant owned writing and terminology, and every one of them worked inside the same gate: nothing shipped that hadn't been explicitly signed off by a human first.

Visual Reference

Illustrative recreation — admin portal, benefit plans list, dense data with clear status states

The production admin and member portals are client-confidential and withheld. Above is an interactive recreation built for this portfolio, using a fictional product name ("Harborview Benefits"), generic plan names, and generalized data — illustrating the same interaction pattern and design-token architecture described below, with no client branding, real names, or real screens reproduced.

Behind the Screens

### One Connected Source, Not Scattered Documents

Separately from the design pipeline, the wider team set up a shared knowledge system that connected requirements, architecture decisions and test plans to each other, instead of letting them live as disconnected documents the way they had for years.

When a business analyst changed a rule, the system immediately showed which diagrams or user stories that change touched, before anyone edited them. Developers picked up implementation work straight from that same connected source, so a feature always traced back to the exact requirement that justified it. Product, design and engineering stopped quietly drifting out of sync with each other, which is the failure mode that usually kills momentum on a project this size.

System Map · D3

### How the Mess Actually Converged

Force-directed graph of how scattered inputs, shifting stakeholder asks and a legacy system with no design function fed into a working agreement and a shared knowledge system, which converged into one design token system, then radiated out to both portals, the Figma library, the generated front-end code, and the pilot that finally got demoed. What shipped

Design Tokens

### One Component, Two Portals, Zero Duplication

Every visual decision, color included, was built as a named token rather than a hardcoded value. That's what let the same button render one accent color in the employer-facing admin portal and a different accent in the member portal without maintaining two separate components.

/* 1. Primitive — the raw brand value (illustrative; not the real client value) */
--brand-primary : #3B5BDB;

/* 2. Semantic layer — theme-aware naming */
--primary : var(--brand-primary) ;

/* 3. Component bridge — what buttons, inputs and cards actually consume */
--ui-primary : var(--primary) ;
.btn-primary { background: var(--ui-primary) ; }

/* 4. Portal-scoped remap — same component, different accent, no duplication */
.member-portal {
--ui-primary : var(--member-accent) ; /* #D97706, illustrative */
}

Four layers, one direction of truth: change the primitive once, and every button, badge and focus ring downstream updates with it, in code and in Figma alike.

Accessibility

### Accessible by Default, Not by Afterthought

Accessibility was a day-one requirement, confirmed before a single wireframe existed, because of who actually uses this kind of software: a third of the member base is over 50, and most employer admins are generalists checking one thing between other tasks, not power users. The target was WCAG 2.2 Level AA across both portals.

Text contrast held to at least 4.5:1, interface elements to 3:1

Every interactive element keeps a visible focus outline

Touch targets stay at 44px or larger throughout

Motion respects the reduced-motion preference

Login avoids anything resembling a cognitive puzzle

Plain-language copy over insurance jargon, member-side

None of that changes the visual language. It just means the design works just as well for the admin glancing at their phone between meetings as it does for someone reading every field carefully.

Measuring Impact

### Proving It Helped, Not Just That It Looked Nicer

Before proposing a redesign, the more useful question was whether we could actually prove it helped. A full year of real usage data gave a solid baseline for how people use the product today, but it could only say how long people stayed, not whether they succeeded at what they came to do.

So alongside the redesign, we proposed a second, smaller set of numbers worth tracking going forward: task success rate per flow, error rate on forms, time to complete a plan configuration, a short satisfaction question after each task, an accessibility conformance score, and a simple self-service-versus-support-call ratio that speaks directly to cost. The goal was never a single "UX score." It was gi

## Replacing Legacy Tools: AI-Powered Blend Optimizer · Dario Espinosa
URL: https://datadaeon.github.io/blendops.html
Summary: Replacing a decades-old Excel model with an ML-driven web app for oil-well fluid optimization. AI-assisted design process using Claude. 7 prototype iterations to React-ready fidelity.

Case Study — Current Project

energy

## Blend Optimizer

Replacing a decades-old Excel-based blend planning workflow with an AI-powered web application , turning oil-well fluid optimization from a manual spreadsheet exercise into a fast, auditable, ML-driven process.

client
Energy Services (NDA)

context
Energy Services

role
UX Lead

stage
Phase 2 · MVP

blend ratio, recalculated live

Excel
replaced entirely

7
prototype versions

3
pilot runs per project

3→1
systems unified

How Might We

// hmw
help Plant Operations Managers run fluid blend optimization faster and more accurately, without losing the nuance and institutional knowledge currently locked inside a complex Excel model?

Context

### The Problem with the Legacy Spreadsheet

The client, a global oil-field services company, operates in completion fluids: engineered salt brine solutions used to maintain pressure in oil and gas wells. Their existing blend optimization process ran through a proprietary spreadsheet model, where engineers manually input well parameters, cross-reference chemical inventories, and calculate optimal formulas for each job.

The model was powerful but brittle: only a few specialists could operate it correctly, results weren't trackable across runs, and every approval workflow ran through email threads and printed sheets. The client's data science team had already built a Machine Learning proof of concept that outperformed the manual approach. The challenge was turning that PoC into a production-ready tool their field ops teams would actually adopt.

The production application is client-confidential. See the interactive recreation further down this page for an illustration of the resulting interface.

My Role

### UX Lead on a Cross-Functional Team

SoftServe was brought in to build the full-stack application: React + Next.js frontend, Python APIs, Azure infrastructure. As UX Lead, I owned the interaction design and prototyping from discovery through Phase 2 MVP handoff — consolidating three disconnected systems into one workflow, working alongside a cross-functional project team.

design approach

Four discovery sessions with the client's operations and data science teams established that the primary user, the Plant Operations Manager , needed a workflow anchored to Jira tickets (the existing job tracking system) and connected to the client's internal plant monitoring system. Every design decision had to make sense within that mental model: jobs → pilots → blend results → approval → lab validation.

AI-Assisted Workflow

AI-accelerated design

### Prototyping with Claude

This project became an active experiment in AI-assisted UX work. Rather than produce static Figma screens, I used Claude (Anthropic) as a design collaborator, describing interaction patterns, iterating on component states, and generating functional HTML prototypes directly from conversation.

The approach compressed iteration cycles significantly: a full-fidelity interactive mockup could be reviewed by engineers and stakeholders within hours of a discovery session, rather than days. By v7, the prototype had accumulated the product's full brand token system, all major user flows, and was close enough to production quality that it directly informed the React implementation.

Component Library

### Building the BlendOps UI Kit

Alongside the prototype work, a dedicated Figma component library was built to give the engineering team a clear, token-driven reference for every UI surface in BlendOps.

The kit covers form controls (dropdowns, number inputs, inline validation), data table patterns (sortable columns, status chips, inline edits), modal flows (confirmation dialogs, optimizer progress, approval submission), and the three-panel shell itself.

Design tokens follow the product's brand palette directly: primary blue for structural authority, cyan for interactive accents, and citron reserved exclusively for commit actions. All components carry accessibility annotations, contrast ratios, and keyboard interaction specs ready for developer handoff.

Figma Variables
Shadcn/ui base
Tailwind tokens
Auto-layout
WCAG AA
Dev handoff specs

// drag to reorder

Token hierarchy drives every decision: structural → interactive → commit action.

Design Decisions

### Why These Choices

component library

Used Shadcn/ui + Tailwind as the component base, building on top of Radix primitives. The interface is data-dense: dense tables, inline chemical formulas, multi-state status chips. That density needed a system that could scale without visual debt, and Shadcn's unstyled base let us apply the product's tokens cleanly.

brand tokens

The product's brand palette maps naturally to information hierarchy: #005495 primary blue for authority and nav, #38C6F4 cyan for accent and topbar stripe, and #DAE24C citron reserved exclusively for primary CTAs such as Run Optimizer, Save to Jira, and Submit for Approval. The citron stands out against both dark and light backgrounds and signals "this commits to action."

typography

Montserrat for UI surfaces (authority, legibility at small sizes in data tables) paired with IBM Plex Mono for values, ticket numbers, chemical formulas, and any data that needs character-level precision. Engineers read mono; it signals trustworthiness for numerical output.

three-panel layout

Left sidebar for job navigation (All Jobs → Current Job → Pilot tabs), center for the active workflow form, right panel for the optimizer result and comparison table. This maps to how operations managers actually work: they hold the job context in their head while checking results against targets. The layout externalizes that mental model.

Stack & Integration

### Technical Context

BlendOps is a standalone Azure-hosted web application. The frontend is React + Next.js; Python APIs handle ML orchestration, Jira sync, and plant-monitoring data retrieval. From a UX perspective, the architecture meant designing around API latency: the optimizer takes 1–2 minutes to return results, requiring explicit loading state design and a clear "run in progress" pattern that doesn't lock the interface.

React Next.js Shadcn/ui Tailwind Python APIs Azure Jira API Plant Monitoring API ML Model Montserrat IBM Plex Mono

// reflection

What surprised me most was how productive the AI-assisted prototyping workflow became once the domain was well-established. The first few iterations were mostly me learning the chemical vocabulary: what density means in ppg vs kg/L, what TCT (Thermodynamic Crystallization Temperature) constrains. Once that was solid, the AI could generate accurate UI scaffolding because I could describe the domain precisely. The quality of the prototype was a direct function of the quality of my domain knowledge. That's a lesson I'll carry forward.

## Daily Bot
Chatbot MVP

MVP chatbot designed to improve cosmetics purchase decisions in online stores, accelerating conversion through an intelligent chat assistant that mimics in-store expert guidance. Research-led, prototype-tested.

Client: PROSCAI (SaaS)
Role: UX Researcher + Designer
Niche: Organic Cosmetics

Problem: Online cosmetics shoppers lack the knowledgeable human guide they'd find in a physical store. This creates decision paralysis, abandoned carts, and low conversion. The Daily Bot replaces that expert with a conversational AI that qualifies needs, recommends products, and converts interest into purchase.

Process

### Research to MVP in 6 Stages

01

#### Benchmark

Competitive analysis of chatbot implementations in cosmetics ecommerce

02

#### Proto-Persona

Defined target user profile: women shopping organic cosmetics online

03

#### Hypotheses

Research hypotheses around decision triggers and conversation patterns

04

#### Interviews

4 qualitative user interviews to validate assumptions and uncover mental models

05

#### Solution

Conversation flow design: question trees, recommendation logic, CTA placement

06

#### 3 Iterations

Progressive prototype refinement based on user testing feedback

Research & Design

Prototype

Chat replaces the human guide at the store. The bot must pattern-match conversational cues to deliver the right recommendation at the right emotional moment. Hesitation signals an unanswered question, not a lost sale.

Outcome

The MVP was built using Landbot.io and demonstrated a complete conversational flow from product discovery to purchase intent. The research validated the core hypothesis: guided chat meaningfully reduces the decision gap in organic cosmetics ecommerce.

## EDGA — A Multi-Agent Design Thinking OS · Dario Espinosa
URL: https://datadaeon.github.io/edga.html
Summary: EDGA — Experience Designer Generalist Agent: a self-built Claude plugin that runs an end-to-end, phase-gated Design Thinking process with a coordinating Overseer, specialized sub-agents, and a continuously-updated knowledge base.

internal tool · founder · claude plugin

## EDGA — A Multi-Agent
Design Thinking Operating System

A self-built Claude Cowork / Claude Code plugin that runs the full Design Thinking process (Empathize through Deliver) as a phase-gated multi-agent system, with a coordinating Overseer, specialized sub-agents for each discipline, and its own continuously-updated knowledge base of UX frameworks and patterns.

context
Internal Tool · Founder

role
Creator · Architect

timeline
2025 – present

platform
Claude Cowork/Code

v3.8 current release

12 KB categories

115+ knowledge notes

9 intake blocks

01 — Overview

Self-Initiated · Internal Tool

### Why I Built EDGA

EDGA — Experience Designer Generalist Agent started from a simple frustration: every real design engagement runs through the same disciplines (research, strategy, systems, prototyping, testing, delivery), but a single chat with an AI assistant has no memory of which phase you're in, no gate to stop you from skipping straight to pixels before the problem is framed, and no persistent record of what was decided and why.

EDGA is my answer to that: a plugin that turns Claude into a small, disciplined studio. One Overseer agent keeps track of where a project is in the process and hands work to the right specialist; the specialists never freelance outside their phase; and every phase ends with a human decision gate, so nothing moves forward without my explicit sign-off.

02 — Architecture

### An Overseer, and a Bench of Specialists

The Overseer is the only agent that talks to me directly and the only one with the full project context. It reads intake data and session memory, decides which phase the project is in, injects the relevant context into a sub-agent, and enforces the human gate before advancing. Sub-agents never load project context on their own. They only work with what the Overseer hands them, which keeps each one focused and keeps token usage predictable on long engagements.

Dario (human gate)

↕

Overseer — phase routing, memory, context injection

↓ hands off, phase by phase

UX Researcher
Empathize/Ideate

Product Strategist
Define/red-team

Systems Designer
Design tokens

Component Builder
Prototype code

Figma Design Auditor
Token/handoff QA

User Testing
Real sessions

Quality Auditor
WCAG/perf audit

Delivery Coordinator
Estimation, git, handoff

↕ (long engagements only)

Memory Coordinator — institutional memory, Obsidian export

Phases are gated: Empathize → Define → Ideate → Prototype → Test → Deliver , each with a documented "artifact contract," a specific output the phase must produce before the gate opens. I approve or send back the work at every gate; the Overseer never advances a phase on its own judgment.

03 — How It's Used

### Three Ways to Engage It

EDGA isn't one-size-fits-all — a quick gut-check and a multi-month retainer need different amounts of ceremony. Onboarding starts with /edga-new , a structured intake across 9 blocks (goals, users, constraints, existing artifacts, timeline, and more) that scopes which mode fits.

MODE 1

Advisory

Fast expert input, no full process

MODE 2

Discovery

Research + framing only

MODE 3

Full Project

All 6 phases, gated end-to-end

For long-running retainers

Projects running past ~3 months switch to a Cycle Model : the Memory Coordinator manages staleness checks and cycle transitions so institutional knowledge about the project doesn't silently rot between sessions. It also handles exporting that project memory to Obsidian for a durable, searchable record outside the chat.

04 — Knowledge Base

### How the Knowledge Base Stays Current

EDGA's sub-agents reason from a generic knowledge base (UX frameworks, research methods, interaction patterns) that grows with every release. New material only gets absorbed through a deliberately slow, checked pipeline, because a design-thinking assistant is only as trustworthy as the sources it's quoting.

01

Deep-research round triggered
Usually kicked off by me forwarding a new source, framework, or paper worth adding.

02

Primary sources read in full
No summarizing a summary. The original paper, book chapter, or spec gets read directly.

03

Citations independently verified
Claims and citations get a separate WebSearch verification pass before they're trusted.

04

Distilled into a capped module
Condensed into a size-capped knowledge doc — never left as sprawling raw notes.

05

Confirmed before absorbing
I get an explicit AskUserQuestion checkpoint before new material is folded into the KB.

06

Written with confidence tags
Findings are marked by how certain they are, not presented as uniform fact.

07

Shipped as a versioned release
Bundled into the next tagged .plugin release with a changelog entry.

05 — Knowledge Base, Mapped

### What the Obsidian Memory Actually Looks Like

Running /edga-export-kb mirrors the plugin's knowledge base into a real Obsidian vault. A Home.md note links out to 12 category Maps of Content (MOCs), each holding the notes for that discipline. The export is content-hash based: it only touches notes that actually changed, never overwrites a note I've hand-edited inside Obsidian, and flags anything orphaned.

Important distinction

This vault is the plugin's own generic knowledge : frameworks and patterns any project can draw on. It is not project memory: a client engagement's institutional memory is a separate export, kept scoped to that one project so nothing crosses between engagements.

## A Token of Gratitude: Token & Session-Burnout Habits for AI Agents · Dario Espinosa
URL: https://datadaeon.github.io/gift-token-habits.html
Summary: A free, portable guide to token and session-hygiene habits for AI code agents — checkpoint discipline, layered memory, and anti-patterns that keep long agent sessions from degrading. Shared as a thank-you for visiting the portfolio.

A Token of Gratitude

## Token & Session-Burnout Habits for AI Code Agents

Thanks for making it this far into my portfolio — as a small thank-you, here's something I actually use day to day: a free, practical set of habits for keeping AI coding agents (Cursor, Claude, or similar) from quietly wasting your tokens and losing the thread on long sessions. No email required, nothing to sign up for.

What it saves you: fewer runaway sessions that burn budget without anyone noticing, less time re-explaining a decision the agent already made ten minutes ago, and fewer "regenerate the whole thing from scratch" cycles once a long session has quietly degraded.

~6 min read
Markdown, portable to any project
Free — no attribution required

⬇ Download the .md file

01 · What This Solves

### What Problem This Solves

Three concrete symptoms, not an abstract fear of "spending tokens":

- Session-memory files grow without limit. If you keep project state in a file like CLAUDE.md / CONTEXT.md / NOTES.md , reading it in full at the start of every session burns context budget before you've even touched the real problem.

- The tool's auto-compact fires late (around 95% of the window). By then the tool decides what to drop, and it systematically keeps mundane output while discarding the reasoning that actually mattered.

- Long sessions re-derive decisions already made in the same conversation, lose track of what was decided ten minutes ago, or drift from the original request. That's context-budget degradation, not "the model got lazy."

This guide attacks the two levers that are actually controllable: tokens per task (well-scoped context) and unnecessary tasks (the Restart Rule, one chat = one task) — not the price per token or the number of users.

02 · Layered Memory

### L0 / L1 / L2 Habits (Abstract-First)

Load information in layers, from less to more detail, and only go deeper once something actually matched the current task.

Level What it is When it loads

L0 The title / first bold line of a state entry, or a doc's title + first paragraph Always — this is what gets scanned to decide relevance

L1 A status log's full entry, a doc's headings, a "where to look" table Only if the L0 matched the current task

L2 The full document, source code, meeting notes, extensive research Only when the task genuinely needs that specific content

Writing rule: every new entry in a state/memory file starts with a bold L0 — one sentence a future session can rank without reading the body. Never open an L2 file because "the name sounds relevant": check its L0/L1 first.

03 · Checkpoint Timing

### Checkpoint at ~60%, Not ~95%

Most agent tools' auto-compact fires around 95% of capacity — by then the tool decides what to drop, keeping mundane output and discarding the reasoning. Intervene earlier, while the agent still has control:

- At ~60% of the session's practical budget (a "this is getting heavy" signal, not an exact token counter).

- Stop at a clean point, not mid-edit.

- Write the state to a file: what was done, what's left, what decision is pending. That's the real checkpoint, not the chat's own memory.

- If a logical unit of work is finished and the code passes its quality gate, commit.

- Say it explicitly: "I recommend a fresh chat from here — the state is saved in [file]/git log."

Explicit handoff: for large or multi-stage work, write the checkpoint as a clearly marked block ("HANDOFF" or similar) with the reference plan, what's done, what's left, and what human confirmation is pending.

04 · The Restart Rule

### Stop Arguing, Respec Instead

If the agent is stuck, produces output that doesn't work, or you find yourself arguing the same point twice — stop arguing. Rewrite the spec (what's being asked, what constraints, what acceptance criteria) and regenerate cleanly. Arguing spends tokens re-deriving; a clean respec spends tokens moving forward.

Corollary: if you correct the same thing twice, that's the signal to write it once as a permanent rule, not to keep correcting it by hand every time.

05 · Memory Writes

### Summary Only, Never the Transcript

Don't paste chat transcripts into durable state/memory files. Writes are summary-level: rationale + outcome, never the full conversation. Every new entry carries its bold L0 and, below it, the minimum needed for another session to understand what happened and why, without reading the original chat.

06 · When to Interrupt

### Escalate on Anomaly, Not on Schedule

Default: autonomous — the agent keeps working and commits without asking permission at every step. Interrupt the human only on a concrete signal:

- the same file rewritten more than ~5 times in a row,

- the build/typecheck fails 3+ times consecutively,

- the tool-call count is roughly 2x the expected baseline for that kind of task.

Don't add a "should I continue?" checkpoint at a fixed number of turns regardless of session health — the goal is for the flow to run mostly unattended, and for an interruption to signal something real.

07 · Scaffolding

### Mechanical Work Is a Script, Not a Session

Creating a new copy/variant of a project (duplicating a folder, renaming identifiers, registering paths across several files) is mechanical work. It's better handled with a shell script than as open-ended, turn-by-turn agentic editing. Only the real design/logic changes inside the new copy need a reasoning model's attention.

Intent note: the moment work starts on a new fork or scoped derivative, write a short note (~5 lines): what changes this round, what stays untouched, and one line answering "fork on disk, or a git branch?" — a full fork only if it needs to run live alongside another version or be published separately; otherwise a branch, deleted once the learning is extracted.

08 · Commit Discipline

### Checkpoint Gated on Build/Typecheck

Commit at the end of the scaffold step, before starting feature edits, and at every natural subtask boundary — but only if the current state passes the project's build/typecheck/tests. If it doesn't pass, commit to a working branch, never to main with broken state.

09 · Plan-First

### Only for Large Work

Write a short plan and get a one-line approval before scaffolding a new variant, preparing a reduced-scope clone, or any refactor touching multiple files. Skip this ceremony for single-file tweaks — it isn't worth it below roughly ~15 expected tool calls.

10 · Indexing

### Soft-Exclude Large, Superseded Trees

Distinguish two levels of exclusion: hard (the agent can't read it even with an explicit mention — binaries, installed dependencies, build artifacts) and soft (out of search by default, but reachable with an explicit mention — superseded versions still useful as historical reference). When something becomes formally superseded, move it to soft exclusion in the same session, instead of leaving it competing for search space indefinitely.

11 · Durable Notes

### A Manual Export Bridge, Never a Database

If a project needs a knowledge layer outside the repo (an Obsidian-style note, a wiki), treat it as a manual, on-request bridge only — never automatic sync, never a source of truth. Export only when explicitly asked, carry minimal metadata, and keep it hand-curated: no relationship queries unless a real index structure exists. The repo's own state files and git history remain the source of truth.

12 · Anti-Patterns

### What Not to Do

- Don't open every file "just in case" — use a "where to look" routing map if one exists.

- Don't paste chat transcripts into durable memory files.

- Don't silently archive a large state file — flag the recommendation and wait for confirmation.

- Don't use broad git commands ( checkout / reset ) on shared work to fix a wrong turn — restore only the agent's own last edit with a targeted patch.

- Don't treat an Obsidian/wiki-style export as a database or source of truth.

- Don't add a "should I continue?" checkpoint at a fixed number of turns.

Install

### How to Install This in Another Project

- Copy the Markdown file into the new repo (e.g., docs/token-burnout-optimization.md ).

- If the agent supports "always-apply" per-file rules, create a summarized 20–30 line version that points to this doc for detail — don't duplicate the full content there.

- If the agent supports "skills" or longer on-demand documents, move the full detail there and leave only the summary in the always-apply rule.

- Adapt the session-memory filenames to the project's actual scheme — none of this requires a particular filename.

- If multiple agents/tools work on the same repo, point all of them at the same doc instead of each keeping its own abbreviated version.

Shared as a small thank-you for visiting my portfolio. No email required, no strings attached — just a set of habits I actually use, written down so they're portable to whatever agent or repo you're working in. If it saves you one runaway session, it's done its job.

— Dario Espinosa

## From Bid to Blacktop: A Field App for Three Different Jobs · Dario Espinosa
URL: https://datadaeon.github.io/gradeline.html
Summary: Designing GradeLine, a mobile-first field platform for a national paving contractor — the sales bid, the dispatcher's desk, and the crew foreman's phone, built through a forked, versioned prototyping pipeline a founder could click through without touching code.

Case Study · In Progress

construction field-ux ai-workflow design-systems current

## From Bid to Blacktop: One Field App for Three Different Jobs

Designing GradeLine , a mobile-first field platform for a national paving and sealcoating contractor — the sales bid, the dispatcher's desk, and the crew foreman's phone in the heat, all one product, built through a forked, versioned prototyping pipeline a founder could click through without touching code.

industry
Paving & Sealcoating

phase
Discovery → Prototype

role
Lead Experience Designer

tags
Field UX AI Workflow

field device, synced live from the job site

8
forked versions shipped

63
catalog components

3
devices, one system

~90%
agent cost is input tokens

How Might We

// hmw
give a sales rep, a dispatcher, and a crew foreman one coherent mobile product, when each works in a completely different context, and the product itself was still being defined underneath us?

The Problem

The client runs paving and sealcoating crews across multiple regions, and the process that got a bid signed, scheduled, and finished still lived across paper tickets, spreadsheets, and phone calls. This engagement started in discovery , which meant the product itself kept shifting week to week — screens that looked settled on Monday were wrong by Thursday because the underlying business logic hadn't been locked yet.

The founder and the client-side stakeholders needed to see and react to real, current thinking constantly, not once a sprint. A static deck couldn't keep up, and asking a non-technical founder to pull a branch and run a dev server wasn't realistic either.

Visual Context

Four screens from across the app — sign-in, dispatch, and the two live-AR surfaces the field crew actually leans on (lot measurement and before/after site verification).

Mobile sign-in & role picker

Live route & dispatch map

Live AR — auto lot measurement

AR ghost-overlay site verification

The production prototypes, Figma libraries, and stakeholder-facing screens are client-confidential and withheld. Everything above is rebuilt for this portfolio with a fictional product name, fictional personas, and generalized data — grounded in the real mobile layouts and the real design-system tokens, but with no client branding, real names, or real screens reproduced.

The Solution

Instead of one prototype that got overwritten every time a decision changed, each meaningful direction became its own full fork of the same React/Tailwind codebase — a complete, independent build, not a feature flag. All forks deployed together as one static, multi-app site, so any version was a public link, not a local checkout.

Underneath every fork sat one living component catalog : the same button, input, badge, and list-row primitives, reused across every version and every persona's screens. That's what kept 8 diverging prototypes from turning into 8 different-looking products.

AI-Assisted Design

### Process and Tools

The same five-stage arc repeated for every version fork, but the AI's role and the tools in hand shifted at each stage — from synthesizing on-site research to shipping a versioned, accessible prototype.

### A Version Switcher a Founder Could Actually Use

Instead of a founder scrolling through Slack screenshots asking "which build is this," every fork got a plain-language label and a running note on what changed. A five-minute click-through replaced a half-hour status meeting. The same screen also had to work for three completely different people — try both controls below.

Illustrative recreation, not the real prototype. Palette follows the real shadcn/ui token set: navy for the one committing action, a scarce light-blue for accents, amber reserved strictly for warnings.

Design System

### One Token Set, Three Platforms

The product design system runs on a white-first shadcn/ui + Tailwind foundation: navy carries every primary call to action at AA contrast, a scarce light blue is reserved for accents, focus, and map detail, and amber is demoted to a single job — the warning state — instead of doubling as a brand color. A shape-and-motion layer on top adapts sheets, radii, and dialog behavior per platform (iOS vs. Android) without touching the brand tokens underneath.

The differentiator was a live map with a custom detection layer showing parcels, routes, and flagged conditions — not a static screenshot, an actually interactive map component in the catalog that every persona's screens could reuse.

navy · primary CTA

blue · scarce accent

light blue · map / focus

amber · warning only

green · success

Process

### Making Cursor and Claude Cheaper to Run

A discovery-phase engagement means the AI-assisted workflow runs constantly, so I spent real time treating token spend as a design problem, not just an engineering one. The biggest lever wasn't the model's output, it was what got loaded into context in the first place — input tokens, not generation, are most of an agent loop's cost.

A few things that actually moved the number: defaulting to a reversible, soft exclusion for files that shouldn't be indexed by default but might still be needed (rather than a hard block that's unreachable even on purpose), preferring diff-based edits over full-file rewrites on anything long, and treating "context rot" as something that happens well before the window is actually full — so context gets loaded just-in-time and abstract-first instead of dumped upfront. Runaway agent loops got an external, mechanical limit — a checkpoint commit — instead of relying on the model to self-police. Prompt caching cut repeated-context cost dramatically, but only holds if the prefix stays stable, which is why the project's own working-memory file got reordered to put the fast-changing "current state" section last instead of first. And a full fork was reserved for anything that had to run live at the same time as everything else; a lighter branch handled exploration that was never going to ship.

Research & Reflection

### What the Field Told Us, and Where It Broke

On-site research surfaced device-shaped gaps, not just screen-shaped ones. A dispatcher at a desk needed the reasoning behind a schedule, not just the result — "why this stop, why now" mattered as much as the assignment itself. A crew foreman's phone, in direct sun, on a schedule, got almost no patience for reading — copy had to be terse and voice-first by default. A sales screen was the one surface a client might actually read, so it was the one place the copy earned the right to be a full, persuasive sentence instead of a fragment. Seven separate on-site findings each traced forward into a specific interface decision this way, rather than sitting in a research deck nobody opened again.

Two honest weak points worth naming rather than hiding: a secondary visual theme prototyped in parallel didn't yet persist a reviewer's style choice across sessions, a known gap flagged for the next milestone rather than a shipped inconsistency. And the fork-per-version model that made stakeholder review painless started to cost real build time once the lineage passed half a dozen versions — every fork was a fully separate application, so the convenience had a compounding price.

None of this ran on one tool. Design reasoning and long-running project memory lived in one AI-agent runtime, implementation happened inside a second, and a separate component-generation workflow used by another teammate ran a third — coordinated through a shared, versioned memory file instead of ad hoc chat threads. On the human side: an engineering counterpart on the client's team, a second frontend developer, and the client's own product approver all worked off the same versioned prototypes and the same catalog, so nobody was ever reacting to a stale screenshot.

// design-decision

Every fork shipped as a real, clickable link, never a slide. That multiplied the deploy surface and the maintenance cost, but a discovery-phase founder acting on a five-minute click-through was worth more than a beautifully-produced deck nobody opened between meetings.

// reflection

The hardest part was never any single screen. It was making three people's genuinely different jobs feel like one coherent product without pretending their jobs were the same job.

## Connecting Businesses: B2B Marketplace Redesign · Dario Espinosa

## Kasuva
B2B Marketplace

B2B online marketplace for Latin America and Spain, co-founded and designed from scratch. Visual identity, UX flows, Magento theme implementation, and frontend HTML template development.

Role: Co-founder & Design Director
Market: LATAM + Spain
Stack: Magento · HTML · CSS

Context: Kasuva was a startup co-founded to address fragmentation in B2B wholesale commerce across Latin America and Spain, markets where businesses still relied heavily on offline catalog browsing and personal relationships. The design challenge was translating that relationship-driven buying behavior into a digital-first marketplace experience.

Full-Scope Design Work

### From Identity to Implementation

As Co-founder and Design Director, ownership spanned the entire design surface: brand identity, UX strategy, UI design, and frontend implementation. There was no handoff: design decisions were made with direct awareness of technical constraints and business requirements.

Brand Identity

Visual Language

UX Flows

Magento Theme

HTML Templates

Frontend CSS

Design

B2B buyers are not impulse purchasers. The UX had to reduce friction in bulk ordering, price negotiation, and repeat purchases, while building the vendor trust that traditionally came from in-person relationship management. The design had to do the job that sales reps used to do.

Context & Role

### Co-Founded and Designed End-to-End

Kasuva was a B2B online marketplace for Latin America and Spain, conceived to connect businesses across regional markets on a Magento platform. As Co-Founder and Design Director, I led both the complete redesign and the frontend development.

- Complete visual and UX redesign of an existing marketplace platform

- Built the HTML template structure and integrated it with Magento

- Designed for Latin American and Spanish B2B buying behavior, which meant different trust signals and navigation patterns than B2C

- Managed design and frontend simultaneously as the sole design resource on the co-founding team

Reflection

Kasuva was the crucible project: co-founding a startup forces design decisions that are real, irreversible, and directly tied to business survival. Every UX choice had a cost. Every redesign iteration was a bet on whether users would respond differently.

The experience of designing and implementing, building the Magento theme and writing the HTML/CSS templates, permanently shaped how I think about design systems. Visual decisions that can't be implemented efficiently are not good decisions. The designer who understands production is a more effective designer.

What Kasuva gave me: a designer-founder perspective that persists in every project since. Build for real constraints. Ship to learn. Redesign with data.

## Exploring the Future: Metaverse Experience · Dario Espinosa
URL: https://datadaeon.github.io/metaverse.html
Summary: Attracted 1,500+ virtual visitors to a fully navigable immersive exhibition at a major European tech convention, designed in 4 months using Spatial and Unity.

Case Study 06

technology

## Metaverse Experience

Designed a metaverse experience that attracted 1,500+ virtual visitors . I got there by solving spatial storytelling for a European tech convention that had no physical constraints to lean on.

period
SoftServe

context
European Tech Convention

role
Lead Designer

tags
Spatial Design XR 3D

visitors, orbiting a shared portal

1,500+
virtual visitors

Spatial
+ Unity

0→1
spatial process

multi
disciplinary team

How Might We

// hmw
design a metaverse experience engaging enough to hold attention without a human guide, for a major European tech convention?

The Problem

A physical convention means one location, a fixed audience, and a time window that closes. The brief was to remove all three constraints. Doing that introduced new problems, though: without spatial affordances, how does a visitor know where to go, what to explore, or how long to stay?

There was no internal process for spatial or metaverse design at the company yet. No templates, no precedent, no established toolchain. The team had to figure out what "done" even looked like before designing for it.

Visual Context

// visual-01

// visual-02

The Solution

Designed the exhibition layout for Spatial + Unity , applying sightline principles borrowed from physical exhibition design to create natural navigation without explicit UI affordances. Visitors moved through the space because the space itself directed them, not because of labels or arrows.

Placed 3D interactive content at focal points, using the company's brand assets to create spatial consistency. The result felt branded without feeling like a trade show booth dropped into 3D.

Spatial Architecture · D3

### Five Layers: From Platform to Visitor

The metaverse experience was designed as 5 distinct layers, moving from the Unity platform through spatial sightlines and branded content moments to the visitor's self-directed journey. Hover each layer.

Key Decision

// design-decision

We prioritized spatial storytelling over information density. An early prototype was overloaded with content, so we stripped it back to 5 key moments. Engagement time increased significantly. In spatial design, less is more measurable than in any other medium.

// reflection

Spatial design is fundamentally different from screen design. There's no scroll, no back button, no obvious hierarchy. You're designing for presence, not just information. The mental shift from 'what does the user see' to 'where does the user look' changed every decision.

## Revolutionizing Data Insights: Dashboard Redesign · Dario Espinosa
URL: https://datadaeon.github.io/nielseniq.html
Summary: Improved feature delivery speed by 30% and cut UX bugs by 50%, after introducing Double Track Agile and a consolidated Figma design system to a burned-out analytics team.

## Dashboard Redesign

Feature delivery sped up by 30% and UX bugs got cut in half. I got there by introducing Double Track Agile and a consolidated Figma design system to a burned-out NielsenIQ design team.

period
6 months

context
Analytics SaaS

role
UX Lead

tags
DesignOps Design Systems Agile

+30%
delivery speed

−50%

40%
user retention

+55%

How Might We

// hmw
eliminate designer burnout caused by reactive, development-driven decision-making, without sacrificing continuous delivery quality?

The Problem

Traditional handoff cycles forced designers to respond to developer decisions rather than lead them. Teams were burning out fixing issues in production rather than driving product strategy.

There was no shared design system, so every designer worked in isolation. More than 60% of design time went into bug fixes, leaving almost no room for discovery or innovation. The team had lost the ability to be proactive.

Visual Context

UX design process flow, from definition through handoff and validation

Sprint board showing design and dev ceremonies across two parallel tracks

The client's product UI itself is confidential. The interactive recreation further down shows the resulting dashboard without any client-identifying detail.

The Solution

Double Track Agile ran discovery and delivery as parallel sprints, formally separating the space where designers could think ahead from the space where they supported delivery. That one structural change ended the reactive loop.

A consolidated Figma design system with tokens, components, and documented variants eliminated inconsistency at the source. Proactive KPI alerts and a democratized data dashboard gave the team visibility to anticipate problems before they reached production.

Process Model · D3

### Double Track Agile: Structural Fix

The swimlane shows how separating Discovery and Delivery tracks ended the reactive loop. Designers stopped responding to developer decisions and started leading them. Hover each cell for detail.

Key Decision

// design-decision

Double Track Agile. The team was stuck in a reactive loop. By formally separating discovery and delivery tracks, designers stopped being responders and became leaders of the product conversation. It was a structural fix to a cultural problem.

// reflection

It started emerging organically, midway through the project. If we'd planned for it from sprint one, the consistency gains would have compounded faster. The lesson: structural process changes need to be designed as deliberately as the product itself.

## From Philosophy to Digital Engagement: Life Coaching Platform · Dario Espinosa
URL: https://datadaeon.github.io/oolalife.html
Summary: Transformed a book tour cancelled by COVID into a mobile-first digital platform with gamified progress tracking — a 7-area gamification framework, 50 user interviews, 4 key personas, shipped in 6 months.

Case Study 04

health & wellness

## Life Coaching Platform

Transformed a book tour cancelled by COVID into a full digital platform built around a 7-area gamification framework , shaped directly by 50 user interviews.

period
6 months

context
Healthcare SaaS

role
UX Lead

tags
Product Design UX Research Web App

7
life areas

50
user interviews

4
key personas

6mo
to MVP

How Might We

// hmw
transform an in-person book promotion experience into a digital platform that captures the same community and personal-transformation value, in 6 months?

The Problem

COVID eliminated the physical event strategy overnight. The OolaLife brand had built its audience through in-person book tours and community gatherings, none of which could happen anymore. There was no digital strategy, no product, and a countdown clock.

The platform needed to serve two distinct user types: Ambassadors with premium access and management capabilities, and regular users seeking personal-growth accountability. Both needed the system to feel human, not transactional.

Objectives & Scope

### Seven Life Areas, One Digital Platform

The founders initially didn't know where to start. They only knew they wanted everything online. Working closely with Dr. Dave Braun and Dr. Troy Amdahl, I defined two interconnected products: a marketing website and a web app with eLearning sections, Ambassador and Coach roles, login, progress tracking, and enrollment built in.

- MVP platform with user enrollment and Ambassador & Coach role hierarchy

- Articles per unit + activities for long-term, monthly, and weekly goal tracking

- Daily Action Steps with built-in accountability and weekly retrospectives

- Dashboard as the main profile page, with progress visible at a glance

- 7 Key Areas: Fitness · Finance · Family · Field (career) · Faith · Friends · Fun

Target audience: Women aged 30–60, high tech literacy, interested in personal development, networking, and Young Living. Competitor references studied: bigskyhealth.com, mindvalley.com, zerofasting.com.

Visual Context

// visual-01

// visual-02

The Solution

Conducted approximately 50 user interviews to define 4 key personas, primarily women aged 30–60 with high tech literacy and strong motivation for personal growth. Research showed accountability mattered more than content quantity.

Designed a gamification system , built from streaks, rewards, progress tracking, and daily action steps, that replicated the social accountability of in-person events. Collaborated directly with clients in live Miro + Figma sessions to compress decision cycles and meet the 6-month deadline.

Research & Process

### From Whiteboard to Wireframe

The primary user journey started at the marketing website and ended at the application. MindValley served as the indirect benchmark. The founders admired its content depth and future-forward positioning, which shaped early explorations of structure and interaction.

- 4 personas co-created directly with Dr. Braun and Dr. Amdahl through collaborative sessions

- Extensive whiteboarding using customer-centric and Design Thinking methodologies

- UX flow maps, wireframing, Information Architecture definition, sitemap, and MVP task scoping

- Mobile-first approach with breakpoints defined early in process

- Oola had organic growth across multiple domains, so we identified a consolidation opportunity for SEO and brand coherence

- SEO strategy and Google Analytics fixes scoped alongside design work

- Accessibility audit and code-level fixes identified and documented

- When the marketing firm joined, aligned digital style guides with their team and Frontend devs

- Handed off to another designer for final delivery; stayed available to close gaps

Project Momentum · D3

### Six Months — Crisis to Launch

Momentum arc across the 6-month project. Each point marks a real milestone, from COVID crisis to the key insight that reshaped the product (accountability > content) to MVP launch. Hover each point for context.

Key Decision

// design-decision

The gamification system was a deliberate bet. Research showed the audience valued accountability above content quantity. They didn't need more to read, they needed a reason to show up tomorrow. The streak mechanic was the product insight, not the feature.

// reflection

Building for an audience that doesn't know they need digital is a different UX challenge than building for tech-native users. You end up teaching people a new language as much as solving a problem for them. The onboarding flow was more important than any individual feature.

OolaLife.com homepage redesign, showing Programs, Products, and the Oola community platform

Oola Lifestyle Excuses, a gamified assessment showing the 7 F's of Oola wheel and life balance score

Discovery research: competitive analysis covering Google, Instagram, Oola site audit, and analytics overview

Mobile login overlay for the Oola app authentication screen, a cellphone-first sign-in flow

## Optimizing User Research at Scale · Dario Espinosa

## Research at Scale

Cut UX research turnaround by 50% . I did it by building research guidelines and AI-integrated synthesis workflows for a construction-SaaS platform's cross-functional product teams.

period

How Might We

// hmw
make rigorous UX research accessible and actionable for designers and PMs who don't have a research background, across multiple product verticals at once?

The Problem

Research was siloed inside the research department. Designers and PMs either waited weeks for research outputs or made decisions without them. The bottleneck wasn't data collection. It was the gap between sessions and actionable insight.

AI tools were available across the organization but unused in any structured research workflow. There were no standardized guidelines enabling designers or PMs to self-serve research at a quality bar the team could trust.

Visual Context

Generic research-process template board

Actual usability-testing session recordings, transcripts, and participant feedback are client-confidential and withheld.

The Solution

Built research guidelines enabling designers and PMs to self-serve qualitative research without a research background. They cover study design, recruitment via Ethnio, session facilitation with UserTesting.com, and synthesis standards.

Introduced AI-assisted synthesis to close the gap between raw sessions and insight delivery. Established cross-functional feedback loops so research findings moved into product decisions in days, not weeks. Deployed across multiple verticals simultaneously.

Research Framework · D3

### Research Process: Definition to Insight

Four-phase research framework built to enable designers and PMs to self-serve UX research without a research background. AI synthesis closed the gap between sessions and actionable insight. Hover each phase.

Key Decision

// design-decision

I introduced AI-assisted synthesis because the bottleneck wasn't data collection. It was the time between sessions and actionable insight. AI cut that gap without reducing quality, as long as it was paired with human judgment at the interpretation layer. Speed without shortcuts.

// reflection

The best outcome wasn't the speed improvement. It was the cultural shift. When designers started asking 'what does the research say?' before writing a user story, the work had done what it was meant to do. Process adoption is the real design deliverable.

## Railway Back Office

Reduced operator task time by 40% and onboarding time by 60%, by redesigning a legacy railway backoffice system with a component-driven design system aligned to Siemens brand standards.

How Might We

// hmw
redesign a complex, legacy backend tool, where every UI decision has safety implications, without disrupting active railroad operations?

The Problem

The PTC Backend Admin Server was a native C++ application with no design standards, cryptic error codes like CSX0256, and zero documentation for onboarding. A train collision made digital modernization non-negotiable. The stakes weren't abstract.

The primary competitor (GE) had already set a high bar for usability. The existing interface couldn't just be iterated on. It needed to be rethought from the ground up, while operators continued to rely on it daily.

Visual Context

Design system reference — colors, UI elements, typography scale

The underlying architecture documents and Figma prototype maps are client-confidential and withheld. The interactive recreation further down shows the resulting interface without any client-identifying detail.

The Solution

Introduced Scrum to a team that had never worked with it, establishing rhythm and predictability for a high-stakes redesign. Built a Material Design UI kit aligned to Siemens brand standards and Flutter-ready component specs using Atomic Design principles.

Dark and light themes. A fully navigable prototype for desktop review. And a separate tablet solution for field workers who needed the same system in motion, on trains, on platforms, in variable light conditions.

System Architecture · D3

### Component Library as Design Hub

Force-directed graph showing how Material Design, Siemens brand standards, WCAG 2.1 AA, and Atomic Design converged into a single component library, which then radiated out to screens, themes, and delivery platforms. Drag any node.

Legacy system
Input frameworks
Component hub
UI screens
Platforms

Key Decision

// design-decision

Flutter had no mature desktop export tool. Rather than block delivery, I designed for web-resolution parity and used Figma + Zeplin for handoff, documenting the gap explicitly for the next phase. Transparency about tooling constraints is a design decision.

// reflection

Doing this solo was the biggest constraint and the biggest lesson. I learned to ruthlessly prioritize what required design leadership versus what could be iterated through developer feedback. The output was cleaner for it, too. Fewer opinions meant fewer compromises.

On Site Collab · POC for Expo

### One Week, One MVP, One Global Stage

During a week-long on-site sprint, the team delivered a fully functional MVP for the C&S Transportation Signals Expo 2021 . The prototype ran live on both a wall-mounted display and a ruggedized tablet, drawing significant interest from railroad operators and sparking the broader vision of merging the BOS tablet capability with the existing desktop platform.

Event photography withheld. The on-site booth and demo stations were client-branded assets outside the scope of what can be shown publicly here.

Design System

### BOS Tablet Design System

The Siemens Trainguard PTC BOS interface required a purpose-built component library designed for operators working in live railroad environments: dense data tables, real-time status indicators, and multi-level navigation across BOS nodes, subdivisions, and locomotives.

The palette is anchored in Siemens Petrol as the structural foundation, with a bright Interactive Teal reserved for live status and active selections. The dark sidebar creates clear spatial hierarchy, letting operators instantly orient within a complex information architecture without visual noise.

All components were designed for tablet-first use, with generous touch targets, high contrast ratios for varying light conditions, and explicit active/inactive/error state coverage across every element.

## Driving Conversions: Electric Vehicle Launch Page · Dario Espinosa
URL: https://datadaeon.github.io/tycan.html
Summary: Conceptual mobile-first landing page for Porsche's Taycan EV. Designed around visceral emotional triggers, conversion rate optimization, and a multi-step pre-order flow. Figma prototype, 2020.

// archive · older work
